def: showing signs that future success is likely; favorable, especially for a beginning
ex: The team's strong first-quarter sales were an auspicious start to Wei's new role as manager.
With clear skies and calm winds, it seemed an auspicious day to launch the new sailboat.

cloze.s: Winning their first three games was an ___ beginning for the new coach.

note: Usually describes beginnings, times, or signs.

def: not supported by any facts or evidence
ex: The rumor that the factory would close turned out to be completely baseless.
Priya's lawyer called the accusations baseless and asked the court to dismiss them.

cloze.s: After a full investigation, the claims of cheating were found to be ___ and were dropped.

def: expressed with force and clarity, leaving no doubt about what is meant
ex: Malik gave an emphatic no when his boss asked if he would work another weekend.
The team's 6–0 victory was an emphatic answer to its critics.

cloze.s: Her refusal was so ___ that nobody dared to raise the question again.

def: confused and jumbled, so that it is hard to understand or follow
ex: After the long overnight flight, Liam was so tired that his speech was nearly incoherent.
Reviewers said the film's plot was incoherent, jumping between storylines without explanation.

cloze.s: The witness was in shock, and her statement to the police was rambling and ___.

def: showing little enthusiasm or interest; half-hearted
ex: The new phone got a lukewarm reception from critics who had expected much more.
Diego's lukewarm response to the vacation plan suggested he had doubts.

cloze.s: Investors gave the proposal a ___ welcome, neither rejecting it nor showing any real excitement.

also: only slightly warm, as with a drink or bathwater that is neither hot nor cold

def: hard to control and tending to behave badly or go off in the wrong direction
ex: The coach kept a close eye on her wayward striker, who often ignored instructions.
A wayward golf ball flew off the course and shattered the clubhouse window.

cloze.s: The mentoring program aims to steer ___ teenagers away from trouble and back toward school.

def: just beginning to exist or develop and not yet mature
ex: The nascent electric-car industry of the early 2000s looked very different from today's market.
Yuki's nascent interest in painting grew into a serious hobby after one summer class.

cloze.s: Government grants helped the ___ startup survive its difficult first year.

def: good at finding clever ways to solve problems, especially when means are limited
ex: Stuck without a tool kit, the resourceful driver patched the leaking hose with duct tape.
Fatima is resourceful; she turned leftover rice and vegetables into a delicious lunch.

cloze.s: Lost without a map or phone, the ___ hikers used the position of the sun to find their way back.

def: showing a cruel lack of concern for other people's feelings or suffering
ex: The company's callous decision to lay off workers by text message drew wide criticism.
It was callous of him to laugh while his friend described the painful accident.

cloze.s: Driving away and leaving the injured cyclist lying in the road was a ___ act.

note: Don't confuse with *callus* (noun), a hardened patch of skin.

def: extremely poor and lacking basic necessities such as food and shelter
ex: The flood left hundreds of families destitute, with no homes and no savings.
The charity provides hot meals and beds for destitute people across the city.

cloze.s: After losing his job and all his savings, he was left ___ and sleeping in his car.

def: harmless and unlikely to offend or upset anyone
ex: What seemed an innocuous question about her weekend made Hannah suddenly uneasy.
Most spiders in the region are innocuous to humans and help control insects.

cloze.s: The joke seemed ___ to him, so he was surprised when it offended several coworkers.

def: acting self-important and grand, often using solemn or showy language to impress others
ex: The pompous speaker talked for an hour about nothing but his own achievements.
Kwame found the restaurant's menu a bit pompous, describing plain toast as 'artisanal grain expression.'

cloze.s: Nobody liked the ___ new manager, who insisted on being called 'Director' and lectured everyone about his degrees.

def: full of noise, confusion, or violent change; very turbulent
ex: The band's tumultuous final year ended in a very public breakup.
The crowd gave the returning champions a tumultuous welcome at the airport.

cloze.s: After a ___ decade of wars and revolutions, the country finally found peace.

def: extremely complicated and difficult to follow
ex: The tax form's instructions were so convoluted that Olga finally hired an accountant.
The movie's convoluted plot left most viewers confused about who the villain was.

cloze.s: His excuse was so ___, full of twists and side stories, that no one believed a word of it.

def: lacking in amount or quality; too small to be enough
ex: On his meager salary, Jamal could barely afford rent and groceries.
The tired hikers shared a meager meal of crackers and a single apple.

cloze.s: Despite months of effort, the fundraiser brought in only a ___ sum of two hundred dollars.

def: having a narrow outlook and concerned only with local matters
ex: Critics said the council's parochial thinking ignored the needs of the wider region.
Traveling abroad helped Sofia move past her parochial views about food.

cloze.s: The editor complained that the paper's coverage was too ___, focused on town gossip instead of world events.

also: relating to a church parish, as in a parochial school run by a local church

def: hostile and aggressive, eager to fight or argue
ex: The belligerent customer shouted at the staff and refused to leave the store.
Their belligerent speeches raised fears of war between the two neighboring countries.

cloze.s: After a few drinks, he became ___ and started picking fights with strangers.

also: as a noun, a nation or group that is fighting in a war

def: having or showing very strong and sincere feeling
ex: Maria is a fervent supporter of the local soccer club and attends every home match.
It was his fervent hope that the whole family would reunite for the holidays.

cloze.s: The candidate's most ___ fans waited in the rain for hours just to hear her speak.

def: persistent and determined, holding firmly to a goal and refusing to give up
ex: Aisha's tenacious phone calls finally got the city to fix the broken streetlights.
The tenacious defender stayed close to the star player for the entire game.

cloze.s: After ten rejections, the ___ inventor kept pitching her idea until a company finally bought it.

def: continuing without stopping, often in an annoying way
ex: The incessant barking from next door kept Tomás awake all night.
Her incessant questions during the movie annoyed everyone sitting nearby.

cloze.s: The ___ rain lasted for nine days without a single break.

def: representing the most perfect or typical example of something
ex: For many fans, a hot dog at a baseball game is the quintessential American summer experience.
With her calm voice and steady hands, she is the quintessential emergency-room nurse.

cloze.s: With its yellow cabs and towering skyscrapers, the scene was the ___ image of New York City.

def: very weak or slight, with little support or substance
ex: The detective admitted that the link between the two crimes was tenuous at best.
After the argument, their friendship seemed to hang by a tenuous thread.

cloze.s: The lawyer argued that the evidence connecting her client to the theft was ___ and unconvincing.

def: having mixed or conflicting feelings about something
ex: Liam felt ambivalent about moving, excited by the new job but sad to leave his friends.
Many residents remain ambivalent about the proposed stadium near the river.

cloze.s: She was ___ about the promotion, pleased by the raise but worried about the longer hours.

note: Means having mixed feelings, not lacking feelings; don't confuse with *apathetic* or *indifferent*.

def: far higher in price or amount than is reasonable
ex: The airport shop charged an exorbitant price for a simple bottle of water.
Wei refused to pay the exorbitant fee the airline wanted for changing his flight.

cloze.s: Rents downtown have become so ___ that many young workers have moved to the suburbs.

def: openly and obviously wrong or offensive, with no attempt to hide it
ex: The referee called a flagrant foul after the player shoved his opponent into the stands.
Dumping chemicals into the river was a flagrant violation of environmental law.

cloze.s: Copying the entire report word for word was a ___ case of plagiarism that no teacher could miss.

note: Not the same as *fragrant*, which means sweet-smelling.

def: impossible to defend or keep up, especially against criticism or pressure
ex: Once the documents became public, the official's position was untenable and she resigned.
Working two jobs while caring for a newborn became an untenable situation for Priya.

cloze.s: Faced with emails proving otherwise, the company's claim that it knew nothing became ___.

def: severe and plain, without comfort, luxury, or decoration
ex: The monks lived in austere rooms with only a narrow bed and a wooden desk.
Her grandfather was an austere man who rarely smiled and never wasted money.

cloze.s: The modern chapel was ___ inside: bare white walls, simple benches, and no ornaments at all.

def: more than is needed or wanted; unnecessary
ex: The editor cut superfluous words to make the news article shorter and clearer.
Now that his phone had a good map app, the paper atlas seemed superfluous to Kwame.

cloze.s: Since everyone already knew and agreed with the plan, a second meeting felt ___.

def: wicked or criminal, especially in a sneaky, scheming way
ex: The hackers sold the stolen data to buyers with nefarious purposes.
In the novel, a nefarious banker secretly plots to ruin the small town.

cloze.s: Police suspected the shell company was a front for ___ activities such as money laundering.

def: lasting for only a very short time
ex: Fame on social media is often ephemeral, gone within a week or two.
The cherry blossoms are beautiful but ephemeral, falling from the trees within days.

cloze.s: Like most viral dance trends, its popularity proved ___, and by next month no one remembered it.

def: lacking energy, brightness, or excitement; dull and uninspiring
ex: After a lackluster first half, the team rallied to win in the final minutes.
Sales were lackluster despite the company's expensive advertising campaign.

cloze.s: The singer gave a ___ performance, barely moving on stage and forgetting several lyrics.

def: bitterly sarcastic and critical in a way meant to sting or hurt
ex: The critic's caustic review called the new musical 'three hours of expensive noise.'
Malik's caustic remarks in meetings made coworkers reluctant to share their ideas.

cloze.s: Known for her ___ wit, the talk-show host mocked nearly every guest who walked on stage.

also: able to burn or eat away material by chemical action, as some drain cleaners can

def: full of energy, excitement, and cheerfulness
ex: The exuberant fans danced in the streets after the final whistle.
Hannah's exuberant toddler ran to the door to greet every visitor.

cloze.s: The ___ graduates threw their caps high in the air and hugged everyone around them.

def: impressive or ambitious in a showy way that is often unrealistic
ex: The mayor's grandiose plan for a floating stadium was never built.
He talked in grandiose terms about becoming a billionaire before he turned thirty.

cloze.s: The ___ mansion, with gold-plated doors and three ballrooms, seemed designed only to show off.

note: Usually negative, suggesting showing off or unrealistic ambition.

def: tired, bored, or cynical after having too much of something
ex: After twenty years covering politics, the reporter had grown jaded about campaign promises.
Even jaded travelers gasp at their first sight of the Grand Canyon.

cloze.s: Having eaten at the world's best restaurants, the ___ food critic was rarely impressed by anything.

def: showing a willingness to take bold, surprising risks; daring, sometimes shockingly so
ex: The climber made an audacious attempt to scale the cliff without any ropes.
Their audacious plan to launch a company in just one month surprised investors.

cloze.s: In an ___ heist, the thieves stole the painting in broad daylight while the guards watched the crowd.

def: not sincere or honest, especially pretending to know less or care more than one really does
ex: It was disingenuous of the company to claim it had never heard of the safety problem.
Jamal found her surprise disingenuous, since she had planned the party herself.

cloze.s: The CEO's claim to be 'shocked' by the losses seemed ___, since internal emails showed he had known for months.

note: Not the opposite of *ingenious*; it is the opposite of *ingenuous* (innocent and sincere).

def: peculiar to one person or thing; unusual and highly individual in style
ex: The professor had an idiosyncratic habit of lecturing in his socks.
The building's idiosyncratic design mixes Gothic towers with bright neon signs.

cloze.s: The chef's ___ menu, pairing chocolate with pickles, reflected her own odd personal tastes.

def: understood or implied without being directly stated
ex: The roommates had a tacit agreement that whoever cooked dinner did not wash the dishes.
By not objecting, the board gave tacit approval to the new hiring plan.

cloze.s: No one ever said it aloud, but there was a ___ understanding that the boss's parking spot was off-limits.

def: done with great care and close attention to every detail
ex: Restoring the damaged painting took the museum team months of painstaking work.
Investigators carried out a painstaking search of the crash site.

cloze.s: After ___ research through thousands of old records, Sofia finally traced her family back to 1820.

def: involving a heavy burden of effort, difficulty, or responsibility
ex: Small business owners complained that the new paperwork rules were onerous.
Caring for three elderly relatives at once was an onerous task for Olga.

cloze.s: The loan came with such ___ terms that the family struggled to make the monthly payments.

def: deserving blame for something wrong or harmful
ex: The court found the driver culpable for the crash because he was texting.
Managers who ignored the warnings are just as culpable as the workers who caused the leak.

cloze.s: The report concluded that the landlord was ___ because he had ignored repeated complaints about the broken heater.

def: friendly and without serious disagreement, especially when settling a dispute or ending a relationship
ex: The couple's divorce was amicable, and they still share holiday dinners with their kids.
The two companies reached an amicable settlement without going to court.

cloze.s: Although they disagreed about the fence, the neighbors reached an ___ agreement over coffee.

note: Usually describes agreements or relationships; *amiable* usually describes a person's pleasant nature.

def: causing deep moral disgust; completely unacceptable
ex: Most people find cruelty to animals abhorrent, whatever the reason given for it.
The idea of cheating was abhorrent to Yuki, even when it would have been easy.

cloze.s: The judge called the attack on the elderly couple an ___ crime that had shocked the whole community.

def: extremely pleasant, peaceful, and picturesque, like an ideal scene
ex: They spent an idyllic week in a small cottage beside the lake.
Diego's childhood on the farm sounds idyllic, though the daily chores were hard.

cloze.s: The village, with its flower-lined lanes and quiet streams, looked ___ in the summer sun.

def: calm and peaceful, not easily excited or disturbed
ex: The lake was placid in the early morning, without a single ripple.
Their placid old dog barely lifted his head during the fireworks.

cloze.s: Even when the toddler screamed and threw his food, the ___ babysitter just smiled and cleaned up.

def: to pass on information, knowledge, or a quality to someone or something
ex: Grandma Wei loved to impart her cooking secrets to anyone who visited her kitchen.
A splash of lemon juice imparts a fresh, bright flavor to the soup.

cloze.s: Good teachers do more than give tests; they ___ a lasting love of learning to their students.

def: to restore someone or something to a former position, rank, or condition
ex: After the investigation cleared her, the nurse was reinstated with back pay.
The city voted to reinstate the late-night bus service that had been cut last year.

cloze.s: The coach agreed to ___ the player to the team once he apologized and served his suspension.

def: to feel deep respect and admiration for someone or something
ex: Many young musicians revere the jazz legends who came before them.
In her village, elders are revered for their wisdom and experience.

cloze.s: Fans ___ the retired goalkeeper so much that they built a statue of him outside the stadium.

def: to trouble someone or something constantly, often with many problems at once
ex: The construction project was beset by delays and rising costs.
Beset by injuries all season, the team finished in last place.

cloze.s: From its first week, the new airport was ___ by problems, from broken baggage belts to flooded runways.

note: Usually used in the passive: 'beset by' or 'beset with' problems.

def: to stop someone from doing what they planned or from succeeding
ex: Quick-thinking staff thwarted the robbery by locking the doors and calling the police.
Bad weather thwarted their plans for a beach wedding.

cloze.s: Security guards managed to ___ the thieves before they could reach the vault.

def: to stop resisting and give in to pressure, temptation, or a strong force
ex: After a week of dieting, Liam succumbed to the smell of fresh donuts.
The town council finally succumbed to public pressure and closed the old factory.

cloze.s: Exhausted after thirty hours awake, she finally ___ to sleep on the train home.

also: to die from an illness or injury, as in 'he succumbed to his wounds'

def: to ask for or try to obtain something, such as money, help, or opinions
ex: The library is soliciting donations to buy new computers for the children's room.
The manager solicited feedback from every employee before changing the schedule.

cloze.s: Before writing the new rules, the council will ___ comments from residents at three public meetings.

def: to make a process or action happen more quickly
ex: Paying an extra fee will expedite your passport application.
The hospital hired more staff to expedite care in the emergency room.

cloze.s: To ___ the move, the family hired three extra movers and packed everything the night before.

def: to fill something up again or restore a supply that has been used
ex: After the long hike, Aisha drank plenty of water to replenish the fluids she had lost.
The grocery store replenishes its shelves every night after closing.

cloze.s: Heavy spring rains helped ___ the reservoir after two years of drought.

def: to make someone feel isolated, unwelcome, or unfriendly, so they withdraw their support
ex: The company risked alienating loyal customers by raising prices so sharply.
His constant boasting alienated his teammates, who stopped passing him the ball.

cloze.s: The singer's rude comments about the city managed to ___ even her most devoted local fans.

def: to spread information or knowledge widely to many people
ex: Health officials used radio broadcasts to disseminate advice about safe drinking water.
The researchers disseminated their findings at conferences around the world.

cloze.s: The school uses a weekly email to ___ news about upcoming events to all parents.

def: to make something impossible or prevent it from happening in advance
ex: His knee injury precludes him from running the marathon this year.
The tight budget precluded any thought of a family vacation.

cloze.s: A lack of funding may ___ the city from building the new library it promised.

def: to persuade someone not to do something
ex: Her parents tried to dissuade her from quitting college to start a band.
Bad reviews dissuaded many people from seeing the film in theaters.

cloze.s: Warning signs about the strong current did not ___ the surfers from heading out.

def: to reduce the value, quality, or importance of something
ex: A few typos did not detract from the strength of Priya's essay.
The loud music detracted from the restaurant's otherwise relaxing charm.

cloze.s: The ugly parking garage next door ___ from the beauty of the old church.

note: Used with *from*. Not the same as *distract*, which means to draw attention away.
